analysis.title: Investment Clock Economic Update, Issue #38: Oil, Chips and Hikes
key_insights: Global growth has been resilient despite higher energy prices, helped by the AI build-out, fiscal support and limited central bank hikes. RLAM expects somewhat slower growth in H2 2026 as higher inflation weighs on real incomes and market interest rates are higher than at the July update.

The base case assumes oil falls gradually from about $100 to about $75 a barrel by late 2027, roughly in line with market pricing. This is a higher path for longer than assumed in July. Scenario probabilities are 60% base, 20% upside (lower energy prices) and 20% downside (bigger, more persistent energy shock with recessions).

Inflation forecasts for 2026 and H1 2027 are raised, and more rate hikes are added: three from the BoE, two more from the ECB (after two hikes), and two more from the Fed (after one hike), with Fed risks skewed to more. These are not seen as large hiking cycles because growth is not demand-driven and booming.

Refined products are the bigger inflation risk than crude. Since end-February crude is up about 50% while diesel (gasoil) is up about 100%. IEA estimates refined product flows through Hormuz are about 60% below pre-war versus about 45% for crude, and Russian refining capacity is damaged. Prices may stay elevated even if the Strait reopens.

Food price forecasts are raised because of fuel and fertiliser costs, a hot and dry European summer and a record-strength El Nino. The effect on CPI is expected mainly in 2027. A food spike could raise inflation expectations and make inflation more persistent.

US consumer spending is the main driver of US growth. It has been supported by tax refunds, wealth effects and a lower savings rate. The savings rate is below pre-pandemic norms, which leaves US consumers vulnerable to shocks, especially an equity market fall. AI explains about 0.4% or less of US growth because much AI capex is spent on imports.

The US breakeven payroll rate (monthly job gains needed to keep unemployment unchanged) is estimated to be near zero, versus about 100k historically. The fall reflects population revisions (about half of the participation drop), ageing (about 10%) and cyclical factors (about 40%). Little job growth could therefore tighten the labour market and lift wages.

US PCE inflation is 3.4% headline and 3.0% core, and the US is in its sixth year of above-target inflation. RLAM sees most upside risk to the Fed forecast, citing the Fed viewing policy as accommodative under Chair Warsh, labour market tightening risk and AI-build-out pressure.

AI is adding some inflation through chip and memory prices, input cost spillovers and data centre electricity demand. The effect on headline CPI is small. BEA's September methodology revision lowered software and accessories inflation, cutting an estimated 0.3pp AI contribution to PCE inflation.

AI labour market effects look modest so far. Recent college graduate unemployment has risen more than average, but cyclical factors, Covid-era over-hiring and remote work are alternative explanations. Sector data show little relationship between AI exposure and payroll changes.

AI financing risk: hyperscaler capex is expected to exceed $1 trillion by 2028 (BoE). Hyperscaler bond issuance in 1H 2026 already exceeded all of 2025. Growing use of private credit and special-purpose vehicles makes leverage harder to assess, and a material earnings shortfall could have market and macro consequences.

Government bond yields have shifted up across the curve in major economies, not only at the long end. Drivers are oil and the Hormuz closure, high debt, weak political will for repair, ageing, more volatile inflation, a possibly higher neutral rate, and hyperscaler issuance. Tighter conditions raise risk for equities when bond-equity correlation is positive.

Fiscal impulse in the US is mostly behind. About $135bn of $166bn IEEPA tariff refunds had been paid by mid-September, and a Fed survey says over 75% of recipient firms plan to keep at least some as cash. Euro area fiscal remains supportive (German plans to borrow over EUR200bn in 2027). The UK is expected to deliver a continuity budget with a modest drag.

Medium-term neutral rate estimates are 3.50% Fed, 3.75% BoE, 2.50% ECB and BoJ. RLAM assumes the ECB and BoE can cut by early 2028. Fiscal dominance and limits from high debt are flagged as possible constraints on central banks.

China: Q2 2026 GDP growth fell to 4.3% y/y, the weakest on record outside Covid. Domestic demand and property remain weak while high-tech exports boom. Late-September stimulus (project loan-rate cuts, smaller-than-expected mortgage subsidies) is seen as modest. Trade tensions with Europe are expected to re-escalate.

Euro area: Q2 GDP rose 0.6% q/q after 0.0% in Q1. September inflation was 3.8%. The ECB raised rates in June and September to a 2.50% deposit rate and RLAM expects two more hikes, with upside risks from gas and food. Gas storage is 68% heading into winter, below the 5-year level.

UK: GDP grew 0.6% q/q in Q1 and 0.5% in Q2, with tentative AI-related gains in services. The labour market is soft and energy bills are expected to rise again in January 2027, pushing inflation above 4% early next year. RLAM expects slower Q4 growth, 1.6% growth in 2026 and three BoE hikes.

Japan: growth has outperformed (1.9% annualised in Q1, 1.4% in Q2) and RLAM expects faster BoJ hikes towards 2%, regardless of oil. US pressure on the yen and Japan's higher bond yields are factors. Hawkish board members Takata and Tamura leave next year, which may slow the pace in 2H 2027.

Political risks: US midterms in November are expected to see Republicans lose the House and possibly the Senate. French presidential election is April 18 (run-off May 2), with Le Pen and Melenchon polling strongly. An early UK election under PM Burnham is possible. Trump has threatened to attack Iran after the midterms.
The multi-asset team stays moderately positive on equities and commodities and negative on government bonds, preferring equities in regions with the strongest earnings such as the US.

sector_views.rationale: Euro area autos are declining under Chinese competition while defence manufacturing is surging. Renault is making military drones and Volkswagen is converting a plant to defence production.

earnings_insights: The multi-asset team notes corporate earnings have been resilient this year and prefers equities in regions with the strongest earnings, such as the US.
A material earnings shortfall at AI-spending hyperscalers is flagged as a risk to markets and the macro economy because of rising debt financing.

risk_factors: Oil and Middle East developments remain the main source of two-sided risk.
Refined product supply and prices stay elevated even if crude falls, and European gas storage is low heading into winter.
A food price shock from higher fuel and fertiliser costs, a hot and dry European summer and a strong El Nino.
US consumer vulnerability given a low savings rate and dependence on equity wealth effects.
Rapid tightening of the US labour market because the breakeven payroll rate is near zero.
AI-related debt financing, private credit and off-balance sheet structures, and a possible earnings shortfall.
Fiscal sustainability and rising bond yields tightening financial conditions.
Second-round inflation effects and more volatile inflation over the medium term.
Political uncertainty from US midterms, the French election and a possible early UK election.
vol_and_positioning: The multi-asset team describes AI as both a boom and a bubble in stock market terms. A burst would hurt US wealth effects and consumer spending.
Higher bond yields can damage equity returns when bond-equity correlation is positive.
geopolitical: Middle East conflict and effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, with IEA estimating flows at about 7.6mb/d in August versus about 20mb/d pre-war.
Trump has threatened to attack Iran after the November midterm elections.
Attacks on Russian refining facilities by Ukraine and Russian export restrictions have cut Russian refining capacity.
Rising EU and China trade tensions, with China agreeing to limit hybrid car exports to Europe.
Taiwan is flagged as a source of a sharp deterioration in relations on any attempt at violent takeover.
US pressure on Japan over yen weakness, including joint currency intervention.
French presidential election on April 18, 2027 with a possible run-off on May 2, and Le Pen and Melenchon wanting to pull back from NATO.

tension_points.bull_case: Fiscal support, AI capex and corporate balance sheets have kept growth and PMIs strong, and could provide more support than forecast, as in the 20% upside scenario with lower energy prices.
tension_points.bear_case: Higher inflation and rates erode real incomes, US savings are low, and an AI-related market fall or energy shock could cause recessions (20% downside scenario).
tension_points.what_invalidates: If energy prices do not fall from here, RLAM would add another hike or two, and a bigger and more persistent energy shock would shift to the downside scenario.

tension_points.theme: US labour market and Fed path
tension_points.bull_case: Breakeven payrolls near zero means the labour market is balanced despite modest job gains and inflation can return to target in 2027.
tension_points.bear_case: Little job growth could tighten the labour market and lift wages, requiring steeper Fed tightening.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A much steeper fall in oil prices would mean central banks hike one or two times less than currently forecast.

theme_stances.key_argument: Even if crude falls or the Strait reopens, refined product prices may stay elevated because Russian refining capacity is unlikely to return quickly.
theme_stances.evidence: refined product prices are likely to remain elevated for some time

theme_stances.key_argument: Inflation risk and resilient growth leave little to stand in the way of modest further hikes by central banks, with the Fed the biggest upside risk.
theme_stances.evidence: More, but not many, rate hikes expected

theme_stances.key_argument: Rising debt, private credit and off-balance sheet structures make AI leverage harder to assess and a earnings shortfall could have macro consequences.
theme_stances.evidence: complex web of financing structures could make it harder to assess the total leverage
